source: We measured mVenus pixel intensity in 327 spines from 11 dopamine neurons and plotted mVenus pixel intensity against spine length (Figure 7G). We observed a weak, but significant correlation between mVenus expression and spine length (R = −0.23, p=2.5e-5).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 7G.

claim: 75% of spines with lengths <2 µm (179 of 240) were scored mVenus positive whereas only 40% of spines longer than 2 µm (33 of 83) displayed detectable mVenus expression.
source: We again categorized spines as mVenus positive if pixel intensity was more than 2 standard deviations greater than the background signal. 75% of spines with lengths <2 µm (179 of 240) were scored mVenus positive whereas only 40% of spines longer than 2 µm (33 of 83) displayed detectable mVenus expression.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text based on analysis of mVenus expression.

claim: Long spines are immature synaptic structures that have few AMPARs.
source: This observation is consistent with the conclusion from our voltage-clamp analyses, that longer spines display smaller AMPAR currents (Figure 6), likely contributing to the smaller uEPSPs observed in current clamp (Figure 4). In total, our data support the hypothesis that the long spines are immature synaptic structures that have few AMPARs.
evidence: This claim is stated as a hypothesis supported by multiple lines of evidence.

claim: In most cases, mVenus-positive shaft synapses outnumbered spines (average density shaft synapses: 2.53 ± 0.14 puncta/10 µm; average density spine synapses: 2.01 ± 0.19 spines/10 µm).
source: Lastly, we compared the relative densities of spines and shaft synapses on individual dendritic segments (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). In most cases, mVenus-positive shaft synapses outnumbered spines (average density shaft synapses: 2.53 ± 0.14 puncta/10 µm; average density spine synapses: 2.01 ± 0.19 spines/10 µm).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were several instances (9/23 dendritic segments) in which shaft synapses and spines were observed in equal numbers, or spines outnumbered shaft synapses.
source: However, there were several instances (9/23 dendritic segments) in which shaft synapses and spines were observed in equal numbers, or spines outnumbered shaft synapses (data were measured from 23 dendritic segments consisting of total of 1525 µm of dendrite, 317 spines and 392 shaft synapses).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs of both structural classes, spines and shaft synapses, coexist and must act together in the integration of synaptic inputs on SNc dopamine neurons.
source: Altogether, these data reveal that excitatory synaptic inputs of both structural classes, spines and shaft synapses, coexist and must act together in the integration of synaptic inputs on SNc dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion from the comparative analysis of spines and shaft synapses.

claim: At hyperpolarized potentials (−60 to −65 mV), the normalized Ca2+ signals in spines were significantly larger in amplitude than analogous shaft Ca2+ signals (normalized Ca2+ signals in spines vs shafts: 0.61 ± 0.03 vs 0.50 ± 0.03; spine, n = 52 measurements, 31 spines; shafts, n = 46 measurements, 21 shafts; p=3.3e-3).
source: Interestingly at hyperpolarized potentials (−60 to −65 mV), the normalized Ca2+ signals in spines were significantly larger in amplitude than analogous shaft Ca2+ signals (normalized Ca2+ signals in spines vs shafts: 0.61 ± 0.03 vs 0.50 ± 0.03; spine, n = 52 measurements, 31 spines; shafts, n = 46 measurements, 21 shafts; p=3.3e-3) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Spine Ca2+ signals were less sensitive to hyperpolarization than shaft signals.
source: Therefore, spine Ca2+ signals were less sensitive to hyperpolarization than shafts signals.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion from the voltage-dependence experiments.

claim: Between −55 to −50 mV, the average normalized amplitude of shaft uEPSPs was 0.71 ± 0.03 (n = 49 measurements from 26 shafts).
source: Between −55 to −50 mV, the average normalized amplitude of shaft uEPSPs was 0.71 ± 0.03 (n = 49 measurements from 26 shafts).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Between −55 to −50 mV, the average normalized amplitude of spine uEPSPs was 1.06 ± 0.11 (significantly larger than normalized shaft uEPSPs, p=0.004, n = 57 measurements from 31 spines).
source: By contrast, the average normalized amplitude of spine uEPSPs was 1.06 ± 0.11 (significantly larger than normalized shaft uEPSPs, p=0.004, n = 57 measurements from 31 spines), indicating that there was strikingly little effect of depolarization on the amplitude of spine uEPSPs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: At hyperpolarized membrane potentials, NMDA receptors are more effectively recruited in spines relative to shaft synapses which may occur through boosting of the voltage in the spine head.
source: This suggests that at hyperpolarized membrane potentials, NMDA receptors are more effectively recruited in spines relative to shaft synapses which we reason may occur through boosting of the voltage in the spine head.
evidence: This claim is stated as a suggestion based on the voltage-dependence data.

claim: When glutamate uncaging shortly preceded an action potential, Ca2+ influx into the spine was dramatically larger than the linear sum of the isolated AP- and glutamate-evoked signals.
source: We found that when glutamate uncaging shortly preceded an action potential, Ca2+ influx into the spine was dramatically larger than the linear sum of the isolated AP- and glutamate-evoked signals (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 9C.

claim: When glutamate uncaging occurred shortly after an AP, spine Ca2+ signals were smaller and resembled the predicted linear sum.
source: In contrast, when glutamate uncaging occurred shortly after an AP (Figure 9D left), spine Ca2+ signals were smaller and resembled the predicted linear sum.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: There was a dramatic enhancement of the spine Ca2+ signal midway through the firing cycle.
source: We measured glutamate-evoked Ca2+ signals throughout the entire pacemaker cycle and found that there was a dramatic enhancement of the spine Ca2+ signal midway through the firing cycle, much earlier than we had expected (Figure 9D right).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The Ca2+ signal was enhanced before the onset of the following AP, suggesting small changes in subthreshold voltage during tonic firing can dramatically influence synaptic Ca2+ influx.
source: Notably, the Ca2+ signal was enhanced before the onset of the following AP (open triangle in Figure 9D), suggesting small changes in subthreshold voltage during tonic firing can dramatically influence synaptic Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 9D.

claim: When glutamate uncaging occurred in the last third of the spike cycle, spine Ca2+ influx was 1.90 ± 0.07 fold larger than Ca2+ influx produced by uncaging alone.
source: When glutamate uncaging occurred in the last third of the spike cycle, spine Ca2+ influx was 1.90 ± 0.07 fold larger than Ca2+ influx produced by uncaging alone.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Linear summation of the AP-evoked and uncaging evoked signals during the last third of the spike cycle predicts signals just 1.28 ± 0.04 fold larger than uncaging alone (measured data was significantly greater than linear sums, p=1.4e-9, n = 58 measurements from 20 spines).
source: By contrast, linear summation of the AP-evoked and uncaging evoked signals during this same range of the spike cycle predicts signals just 1.28 ± 0.04 fold larger than uncaging alone (measured data was significantly greater than linear sums, p=1.4e-9, n = 58 measurements from 20 spines).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: Subthreshold voltage alone is sufficient to enhance glutamate-evoked Ca2+ influx.
source: However, we wanted to determine if the subthreshold voltage alone was sufficient to enhance glutamate-evoked Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This claim is stated as a question that was tested experimentally.

claim: Dramatic enhancement of spine Ca2+ influx was observed in the middle and late phases of the spike cycle when measuring peak Ca2+ signals before the onset of spikes (middle phase: measured Ca2+ = 1.67 ± 0.07, linear sum = 0.95 ± 0.03, p=5.5e-12, n = 41 measurements from 20 spines; late phase: measured Ca2+ = 1.64 ± 0.07, linear sum = 0.85 ± 0.04, p=2.7e-13, n = 36 measurements from 20 spines).
source: Using this alternative measure, we observed dramatic enhancement of spine Ca2+ influx in the middle and late phases of the spike cycle (middle phase: measured Ca2+ = 1.67 ± 0.07, linear sum = 0.95 ± 0.03, p=5.5e-12, n = 41 measurements from 20 spines; late phase: measured Ca2+ = 1.64 ± 0.07, linear sum = 0.85 ± 0.04, p=2.7e-13, n = 36 measurements from 20 spines).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support.

claim: Glutamate-evoked spine Ca2+ influx in dopamine neurons is enhanced in a time window that occurs periodically during the natural pacemaker cycle.
source: Therefore, we find that glutamate-evoked spine Ca2+ influx in dopamine neurons is enhanced in a time window that occurs periodically during the natural pacemaker cycle.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion from the pacemaking experiments.

claim: Application of TTX reduced the spine Ca2+ signal by 25 ± 10.0% (p=0.039).
source: On average, TTX reduced the spine Ca2+ signal by 25 ± 10.0% (p=0.039, student's paired) (Figure 10B) but had little effect on dendritic Ca2+ signals (reduced by 9 ± 10%, p=0.45) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 10B.

claim: TTX had little effect on dendritic Ca2+ signals (reduced by 9 ± 10%, p=0.45).
source: On average, TTX reduced the spine Ca2+ signal by 25 ± 10.0% (p=0.039, student's paired) (Figure 10B) but had little effect on dendritic Ca2+ signals (reduced by 9 ± 10%, p=0.45) (Figure 10C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Sodium channels play a role in boosting synaptic potentials in spines of substantia nigra dopamine neurons.
source: Therefore, in addition to the known involvement of sodium channels in enabling robust backpropagation of action potentials in the dendrites of dopamine neurons (Gentet and Williams, 2007; Hausser et al., 1995), we find a likely role of sodium channels in boosting synaptic potentials in spines of substantia nigra dopamine neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion from the TTX experiments and supported by citations.

claim: Blockade of NMDA receptors with D-AP5 (50 µM) reduced spine Ca2+ influx by 49 ± 6% (p=2.2e-3).
source: On average, blockade of NMDA receptors reduced spine Ca2+ influx by 49 ± 6% (p=2.2e-3) (Figure 10E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 10E.

claim: The effect of D-AP5 on the dendrite Ca2+ signal was smaller, on average reduced by 36 ± 10% (p=0.02).
source: The effect of D-AP5 on the dendrite Ca2+ signal was smaller, on average reduced by 36 ± 10% (p=0.02) (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text with statistical support and shown in Figure 10F.

claim: TTX and D-AP5 produced greater attenuation of the spine Ca2+ signal than the dendritic Ca2+ signal, suggesting greater activation of NMDA receptors and voltage-dependent channels in the spine head than the dendrite in response to glutamate uncaging.
source: The finding that TTX and D-AP5 produced greater attenuation of the spine Ca2+ signal than the dendritic Ca2+ signal suggests that there is greater activation of NMDA receptors and voltage-dependent channels in the spine head than the dendrite in response to glutamate uncaging.
evidence: This claim is stated as a suggestion based on the pharmacological experiments.

claim: The contribution of voltage-gated channels to glutamate-evoked responses provides a mechanism by which subtle changes in the subthreshold voltage can shape the synaptic responses of dendritic spines.
source: The contribution of voltage-gated channels to glutamate-evoked responses provides a mechanism by which subtle changes in the subthreshold voltage—like those observed during tonic firing—can shape the synaptic responses of dendritic spines.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Dendritic spines are present on substantia nigra dopamine neurons both in live and in fast-perfusion fixed tissue.
source: We show that dendritic spines are present on substantia nigra dopamine neurons both in live and in fast-perfusion fixed tissue.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: In PSD-95 mVenus mice, spines were present at densities only slightly lower than shaft synapses.
source: In PSD-95 mVenus mice, spines were present at densities only slightly lower than shaft synapses.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Electrical stimulation of presynaptic inputs resulted in Ca2+ influx into the spine head demonstrating that spines are innervated by terminals and act as functional sites of synaptic transmission.
source: Importantly, electrical stimulation of presynaptic inputs resulted in Ca2+ influx into the spine head demonstrating that spines are innervated by terminals and act as functional sites of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Activation of long-necked spines results in small amplitude uEPSPs due in part to a lower AMPA/NMDA ratio and higher spine neck resistance.
source: Testing individual spines with glutamate uncaging, we show that activation of long-necked spines results in small amplitude uEPSPs due in part to a lower AMPA/NMDA ratio and higher spine neck resistance.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Stronger electrical compartmentalization in spines results in boosting of the spine voltage.
source: We demonstrate that stronger electrical compartmentalization in spines results in boosting of the spine voltage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Activating spines during tonic firing leads to enhancement of spine Ca2+ that occurs periodically in a window starting at the middle phase and lasts throughout remainder of the spike cycle.
source: Lastly, activating spines during tonic firing, we found that spine Ca2+ signals are dramatically enhanced during the middle phase of the interspike interval, independent of action potentials. This enhancement of spine Ca2+ results from strong recruitment of NMDA receptors and voltage-gated channels, likely due to boosting of the spine voltage. Therefore, these results show that in addition to shaft synapses, a meaningful source of excitation of SNc arrives via synaptic inputs onto dendritic spines.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The enhancement of spine Ca2+ during tonic firing results from strong recruitment of NMDA receptors and voltage-gated channels, likely due to boosting of the spine voltage.
source: This enhancement of spine Ca2+ results from strong recruitment of NMDA receptors and voltage-gated channels, likely due to boosting of the spine voltage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: A meaningful source of excitation of SNc arrives via synaptic inputs onto dendritic spines.
source: Therefore, these results show that in addition to shaft synapses, a meaningful source of excitation of SNc arrives via synaptic inputs onto dendritic spines.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The spine density values reported are in close agreement with a recent study of dopamine neurons spines in juvenile mice.
source: These values are also in close agreement with a recent study of dopamine neurons spines in juvenile mice (Jang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The density of spines on dopamine neurons is considerably lower than pyramidal neurons (typically >10 spines/10 μm) but similar to some GABAergic interneurons neurons of the hippocampus and cortex that have spine densities of 2–4 spines/10 μm.
source: The density of spines on dopamine neurons is considerably lower than pyramidal neurons (typically >10 spines/10 μm) but similar to some GABAergic interneurons neurons of the hippocampus and cortex that have spine densities of 2–4 spines/10 μm (Kawaguchi et al., 2006; Scheuss and Bonhoeffer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Up to 70% of synaptic inputs that are received by the SNc dopamine neurons are inhibitory while a much smaller fraction of the synaptic inputs arrive from excitatory sources.
source: Up to 70% of synaptic inputs that are received by the SNc dopamine neurons are inhibitory while a much smaller fraction of the synaptic inputs arrive from excitatory sources (Bolam and Smith, 1991; Henny et al., 2012; Smith et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The low density of dendritic spines on SNc dopamine neurons may simply reflect the low density of excitatory inputs overall.
source: This raises the possibility that the low density of dendritic spines on SNc dopamine neurons may simply reflect the low density of excitatory inputs overall.
evidence: This claim is stated as a possibility in the Discussion.

claim: The ratio of spines to PSD95-mVenus positive shaft puncta is 4 to 5.
source: Consistent with this idea, we find that the ratio of spines to PSD95-mVenus positive shaft puncta is 4 to 5.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion based on experimental observations.

claim: Despite a low absolute density of spines on dopamine neurons, the relative density of shaft and spine synapses is comparable.
source: Therefore, despite a low absolute density of spines on dopamine neurons, the relative density of shaft and spine synapses is comparable.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.

claim: If only spines shorter than 1.2 μm are considered, there is no significant correlation between spine length and uEPSP amplitude (Pearson's R = −0.054; n = 21 spines; p=0.81).
source: However if we only consider spines shorter than 1.2 μm, we also observe no significant correlation between spine length and uEPSP amplitude (Pearson's R = −0.054; n = 21 spines; p=0.81).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion with statistical support.

claim: Spine sodium channels may function to reduce variability in spine potentials, Ca2+ influx and subsequent neurotransmitter release from spines.
source: As Bywalez et al. proposed, the spine sodium channels may function to reduce variability in spine potentials, Ca2+ influx and subsequent neurotransmitter release from spines.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion as a proposal from another study.

claim: During pacemaking in dopamine neurons, the interspike membrane potential covers a narrow but relatively depolarized subthreshold voltage range with an average non-spike voltage of ~-55 mV.
source: However, during pacemaking in dopamine neurons, the interspike membrane potential covers a narrow but relatively depolarized subthreshold voltage range with an average non-spike voltage of ~-55 mV (Hage and Khaliq, 2015).

claim: At depolarized voltages around -55 mV, the membrane potential is within the steepest region of the voltage-activation curve of sodium channels, where even a small amplification of the spine head EPSP may lead to significant sodium channel activation.
source: At these depolarized voltages, the membrane potential is within the steepest region of the voltage-activation curve of sodium channels, where even a small amplification of the spine head EPSP may lead to significant sodium channel activation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion based on knowledge of sodium channel properties.

claim: EPSPs of 5 mV can lead to activation of both persistent and transient sodium current.
source: In a clear demonstration of the relationship of EPSPs with voltage-gated sodium channels, Carter et al. (2012) showed that EPSPs of 5 mV can lead to activation of both persistent and transient sodium current.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Even if the effects of the spine neck resistance on electrical signaling are small, the intrinsic properties of dopamine neurons may allow minor amplification to produce major effects on the synaptic voltage response.
source: Therefore, even if the effects of the spine neck resistance on electrical signaling are small, the intrinsic properties of dopamine neurons may allow minor amplification to produce major effects on the synaptic voltage response.
evidence: This claim is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion.
